extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for conducting valid reasoning, inductive inference, and representative measurement in the empirical sciences. Focuses on the mental powers, fundamental logical laws, the role of likeness/identity in inference, and the use of proxies/instruments for measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Identity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a fundamental axiom of thought: an entity is identical with itself and this self-evidence is a foundational basis for reasoning. The law is to be assumed as a prior condition for logical development rather than derived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: "A thing cannot both be and not be."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as a primary axiom (Aristotle): contradictory attributes cannot both belong to the same object at the same time and place. Used as a self-evident foundation for valid assertions and to avoid contradictory conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Duality (Excluded Middle)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A thing must either be or not be."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts two alternatives at every step (presence/absence, affirmation/negation) and that there is no third alternative between opposites. Complements the other two laws to give reasoning its dual character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers of mind required for scientific method
rubrics_metrics.description: The mental faculties relevant to acquiring knowledge are three: (1) The Power of Discrimination; (2) The Power of Detecting Identity; (3) The Power of Retention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each power has a distinct role: discrimination distinguishes sensations; identity detection unifies experiences into generalisations; retention (memory) stores records. Science requires not only discrimination but the capacity to detect sameness and retain it to enable inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference depends on sufficient likeness/identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Inference rule: "so far as there exists sameness, identity or likeness, what is true of one thing will be true of the other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central difficulty is determining whether there exists a sufficient degree of likeness to warrant inference. This criterion underpins all forms of induction and substitution-based reasoning; validity rests on adequate similarity between instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of samples/proxies (substitutive reasoning) for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: A sample or proxy that exactly represents qualities of one instance may be used to infer properties of another (e.g., a sample to represent texture, a standard measure to compare lengths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative substitution is valid when the proxy truly stands for the quality measured. Examples: using a sample of cloth to judge the whole, a staff/foot-rule to compare lengths, a tuning-fork to compare pitch. Emphasises that the proxy must represent the relevant attribute exactly for the inference to hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative measurement extends sensory limits via instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruments and indirect devices can register or stand for quantities beyond direct perception (e.g., siren to count vibrations, liquids matching refractive index).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructing an appropriate instrument or proxy (siren, tuning-fork, matching-liquid) and adjusting it into agreement with the phenomenon permits measurement by substitution. Successful representative measurement requires that the instrument's measured property corresponds accurately to the target property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of correspondence between signs/words and things
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic treats signs and symbols as instruments of reasoning which must correspond to the thoughts and objects they represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While logic uses language and symbols, their legitimacy depends on faithful correspondence to thoughts and external objects. Reasoning/presentation requires clear material signs so ideas can be discussed and verified by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of axioms/rules in concrete objects for applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms and rules of mathematical/scientific science must be verified in concrete objects for calculations founded upon them to have validity or utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical rules attain utility only once checked against observable reality; the ultimate objects of mathematical or logical science are the things themselves, not mere symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of induction due to limited experience and hidden differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Because experience is limited, similar outward appearances may conceal hidden differences; we can never be sure no new instances will occur to refute our inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inductive confidence increases with wider experience and better examination but never guarantees certainty. Practically, more extensive and well-reasoned knowledge reduces the probability of inductive failure; exceptions often get reduced to law as investigation proceeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of thought are prescriptive standards, not guarantees of correct reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Although called necessary laws, laws of thought are what the mind ought to obey; mistakes in reasoning are frequent and the logician must acknowledge fallibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logicians should account for human error: the existence of laws does not imply minds always obey them. Recognition of frequent mistakes justifies careful development of rules and methods to detect and correct errors through comparison with events of objective nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitutive process is universally applicable to measurement and comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The same principle of substitution (using a third representative item) applies across qualities — length, sound, weight, refractive power — enabling measurement and comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate generality: staff or rule for length, tuning-fork linking distant organ pitches, siren for vibration counts, matching liquid for refractive index. The criterion is that substitution preserves the relevant attribute for comparison or measurement.
